headline_marked: China's [[LineShine]] supercomputer reclaims world's fastest title, exceeding 2 exaflops
headline: China's LineShine supercomputer reclaims world's fastest title, exceeding 2 exaflops
summary: The new machine hit 2.198 Exaflops, surpassing the US's El Capitan and marking China's return to the top spot for the first time since 2017.
details: China has once again claimed the title of the world's fastest supercomputer with its new 'LineShine' machine, achieving a performance of 2.198 Exaflops. This surpasses the previous record holder, the USA's El Capitan, which achieved 1.809 Exaflops.

LineShine is the first supercomputer to exceed two exaflops of sustained double-precision performance using CPUs only. It achieves this feat without relying on GPUs, instead utilizing a custom 304-core processor with 13.79 million cores.

The new ranking features five systems that have breached the exascale threshold. These include one in China, three in the US (including Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Frontier at No. 3 and Aurora at No. 4), and one in Germany (Jupiter Booster at No. 5).

Despite technology embargoes, China's success highlights architectural diversity in supercomputing. The Top500 list shows various approaches, including Intel, AMD, NVIDIA, and custom accelerators, indicating no single dominant technology path.

Unlike many of China's previous supercomputers, LineShine was developed without public funding. This allowed its designers to submit the machine for Top500 testing, though certain details like the CPU manufacturer and chip technology remain undisclosed.
caption:
China's LineShine supercomputer is now the world's fastest, hitting 2.198 Exaflops and reclaiming the top spot for the first time in six years.

China has once again claimed the title of the world's fastest supercomputer with its new 'LineShine' machine, achieving a performance of 2.198 Exaflops. This surpasses the previous record holder, the USA's El Capitan, which achieved 1.809 Exaflops.

LineShine is the first supercomputer to exceed two exaflops of sustained double-precision performance using CPUs only. It achieves this feat without relying on GPUs, instead utilizing a custom 304-core processor with 13.79 million cores.

The new ranking features five systems that have breached the exascale threshold. These include one in China, three in the US (including Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Frontier at No. 3 and Aurora at No. 4), and one in Germany (Jupiter Booster at No. 5).

Despite technology embargoes, China's success highlights architectural diversity in supercomputing. The Top500 list shows various approaches, including Intel, AMD, NVIDIA, and custom accelerators, indicating no single dominant technology path.

Unlike many of China's previous supercomputers, LineShine was developed without public funding. This allowed its designers to submit the machine for Top500 testing, though certain details like the CPU manufacturer and chip technology remain undisclosed.
